1:
What the opening verb tells them to do is unusually disputed. Gill takes it of a solemn assembly, the people gathering to the temple and to their synagogues to humble themselves and pray that God would avert his judgments; but he reports another rendering, first adorn yourselves and then others, as the Talmud has it, which he says comes to the same as the word of Christ about casting the beam out of one's own eye first. Ellicott says the received rendering has little to recommend it, and offers two possibilities from the obscure verb, sift yourselves, meaning winnow out the sins which have roused the anger of Jehovah, or bend yourselves, which he prefers, the contumacious nation being told to bend in submission before the judgment is revealed. Clarke gives the sifting sense, separate the chaff from the wheat before the judgments fall.

Calvin argues the point out. He notes that interpreters differ over the root, some deriving it from a verb meaning to search and some from the noun for chaff, and he rejects the refined reading which makes the prophet say gather the chaff, gather the chaff, in ridicule of the people's empty confidence. He holds that the plain sense is gather yourselves, because that is what the grammatical construction requires, and that the figure is answered in the next verse: the day of your scattering is at hand, when you will vanish away like chaff; so while God withholds his hand, gather yourselves that you may not be dissipated. Behind it he sets a general rule, that God fulminates in his word against men in order that he may withhold his hand from them, and that the more severely he sets his wrath before us, the more clearly he testifies how dear our salvation is to him.

Henry makes the same observation from the placing of the call. He says the design of the terrible chapter before it was not to drive the people to despair but to drive them to God and to their duty, not to frighten them out of their wits but out of their sins; and he contrasts the counsel given when the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans was decreed, that those in Judea should flee to the mountains, whereas here they are told to come together, since God warns that he may not wound. Henry also passes on the reading enquire into yourselves, search and try your ways, that you may find out the sin by which God has been provoked.

The nation not desired is read three ways. Henry allows both not desiring, of a people with no mind to repent, who are told to come together and see whether they can stir up desires in one another, and not desirable, since a land that had been a land of delight was now unlovely. Clarke and Wesley keep the second, Wesley adding that they were unwilling to return and unworthy to be received. Ellicott takes it otherwise again, as a nation not abashed by the threats of God, the shameless and defiant nation, and says the seventy read it so.

The urgency of the second verse turns on a figure of birth. Gill compares the decree to a woman ready to be delivered, pregnant with wrath and just ripe for execution; he denies that anything the people did could frustrate it, and says only that those who repented might be saved from the general calamity. Ellicott sees no occasion to identify the decree with the book of the law brought to light at the reformation under Josiah, and prefers to take the next clause parenthetically, that the day is passing by like chaff whirled before the wind. Keil and Delitzsch sets out the chapter as a call to repentance supported by two reasons, the coming overthrow of the surrounding nations and the punishment awaiting Jerusalem itself.
3:
Who the meek are is settled from the word itself. Calvin explains that the Hebrews derive the noun from a verb meaning to afflict or to be humble, so that by a metaphor the meek are those who have been subdued; abundance commonly produces insolence, but by adversity men learn to become meek. The wicked may be smitten and still keep a stiff and iron neck and a brazen front, whereas the faithful are tamed, as Jeremiah confesses of himself that he was like an untamed heifer before he was chastised. Clarke renders it the oppressed and humbled of the land, and Wesley simply the humble ones. Gill reads them as the remnant according to the election of grace, for whose sake the general exhortations to repentance are given out at all, since they alone would profit by them; he describes them as having a true sense of sin, and, conscious of the imperfection of their own righteousness, submitting to the righteousness of Christ.

Why the address narrows to a few is Calvin's own explanation. He says the prophet turned to a small number because he saw he could produce no effect on the promiscuous multitude. From this he draws a rule for ministers, that though they may think they spend their labour to no purpose while they sing to the deaf, as the proverb is, they ought not to depart from their vocation, since there will always be some who show after a long time that they had been divinely saved. He adds that when God raises his voice some harden others, so that men lead one another into ruin; the faithful are not to regard what the multitude does, but to come without delay when God gives them a hope of pardon.

That those already doing right are told to seek is the difficulty of the verse. Calvin states it plainly, that the two clauses seem inconsistent, since a people who had formed their life by the rule of uprightness would need no such exhortation. He answers it twice over. Even the best are roused by God's scourges to seek true religion with greater ardour, because none of us fully performs his duty. And faith is grievously tried when good and wicked are chastised without any difference, the godly being tempted to think it has availed them nothing to have served God sincerely; so they are exhorted to persevere, since in the first confusion no difference would appear, but the end would not be the same, and their patience would at length find that he is a just judge who delivers his people in their extremity.

What the seeking consists of is then defined. Calvin says that to do the judgment of God here is to form the life according to the righteousness of the law, the word sometimes designating the punishment allotted to the wicked but frequently meaning equity or the rule of right living, and being called the judgment of God because it is what he prescribes in his word. He warns against the shorter way, that hypocrites as soon as God invites them accumulate many rites and weary themselves in things of no value, thinking they have sufficiently sought God when they have performed a number of ceremonies. Humility is joined to righteousness, he adds, because it is difficult even for the best of men not to murmur when God chastises them severely, so that the faithful are to bear patiently the rigour by which he tries them, as Peter also bids us humble ourselves under the mighty hand of God. Ellicott glosses the same clause as executed his sentence, that is, acted in compliance with his revealed will by refraining from the sins named earlier.

On the closing words Clarke says the sword has not a commission against such, and Wesley that they are hid under the wing of divine providence.
4:
Why an oracle against the Philistines follows the call to repentance is answered several ways. Gill reports the connection made by Aben Ezra, that the word at the head of the verse joins it to the exhortation, so that they are to seek the Lord and not the Philistines, since it would be vain to flee thither for shelter; others take it as alleviating their calamity, since their enemies would have no occasion to insult them. Wesley puts it plainly, that it is time to seek God because the neighbours will be destroyed as well as they. Keil and Delitzsch treats the verse as the hinge, tied by that same word to the exhortation and introducing the threat that opens with the woe. Calvin takes it as the beginning of consolation for the elect: God's vengeance on his own people would last only for a time and would then be transferred to other nations, preserving the remnant chosen as a seed, that some church might remain. He adds why the faithful needed telling: when the Lord spares the wicked and chastens us, we are tempted to think nothing better than to shake off every yoke.

Henry gives the same double purpose. The prophecy was meant to awaken the Jews by making them sensible how large the inundation of calamities would be, and to comfort them that their case, though sad, would not be singular, since the wretched find it consolatory to have companions of their woe; and that though God had seemed to be their enemy he was still an enemy to their enemies. Henry observes that of the five lordships only four are named, some thinking Gath is left out because it was by then subject to Judah; and that the Philistine country is called Canaan because it was named in the grant made to Israel, whom they wrongfully kept out of possession. Though the rights of others may be long detained unjustly, he adds, the righteous God will at length avenge the wrong.

The form of the verse is noticed by several. Gill says there is a beautiful play on words not to be expressed in English; Ellicott identifies it as a paronomasia in the first and last cities, forsaken and rooted up echoing the names themselves; Calvin observes that the first and last lines correspond in sound. On the words at noon day, Ellicott says the city would be so defenceless that there would be no need to surprise it at night, and Wesley that it would be taken by force at noon by the Babylonians. Ellicott traces what became of the cities: Gaza captured by Alexander the Great after a two months' siege and re-peopled, destroyed later by Antiochus for its fidelity to Ptolemy, razed again and rebuilt, and assigned by the Romans to the kingdom of Herod; Ashdod, the Greek Azotus, destroyed by the Maccabees and not restored until a Roman governor rebuilt it. Clarke keeps to the older fulfilment, that the Philistines were ruined by Nebuchadnezzar about the time he took Tyre.

The Cherethites are variously identified. Gill reports from Kimchi and Ben Melech that the name covers the Philistines in general, or a tribe in the south of their country, and recalls that from this nation the bodyguard of David and Solomon was drawn, a band which as Josephus says never departed from the king's person. The Greek version calls them strangers of the Cretians, and some take them for a colony from Crete; Gill argues the reverse, that Crete was the colony, since the Arabians call the country of the Philistines Keritha and the Syrians Creth. Clarke and Ellicott allow the Cretan connection, while Wesley renders the name destroyers, men terrible to their neighbours. Ellicott adds that Canaan originally means low-lying ground and here indicates the maritime plain the Philistines held.
6:
One word in the description of the ruined coast is unsettled. Calvin says it does not mean sheepcots but digging, and that the reference is either to pits dug for watering the flock or to caves dug for shelter; he gives as the easiest construction dwellings, the digging of shepherds, and reports that Eastern shepherds use caves very frequently, sleeping in them and driving their flocks into them at night. Gill offers the same two senses, ditches dug to receive rainwater or cottages dug in subterraneous places to shelter shepherds from the sun, and adds that some were large enough to take in the flocks, citing the cave in which the sheep and goats of Polyphemus lay down and slept, and the caverns used in Iceland to secure them from the cold. Ellicott declines both, rendering the phrase places for shepherds' pastures, taking the word as a plural of one meaning pasture, with a play on the name of the Cherethites in the verse before. Clarke reports a third course, that Newcome takes the word as a proper name rather than cottages or folds, and that the Greek and Syriac read it as Crete; Secker notes that the word is not found elsewhere and probably names the Cherethim country.

The picture itself is not disputed. Wesley says that instead of cities full of rich citizens there shall be only cottages for shepherds, and Gill that instead of towns full of merchants and warehouses full of goods, a few huts would be seen where shepherds sheltered from the heat by day. Calvin gives the reason: when a country is without inhabitants shepherds occupy it, for there is no sowing nor reaping there and grass alone grows, so that where there is no cultivation they find a place for their flocks.

The turn to Judah is what Calvin dwells on. He calls it a striking divergence from the flocks of shepherds to the tribe of Judah, which was itself the chosen flock of God, the prophet having said the region would be waste and then adding that the waste would be for the benefit of the chosen people. He also observes that the promise is confined to a remnant, since the greater part had become irreclaimable; but the mentioning of a remnant shows there would always be some seed from which God would raise up a new church, and is meant to keep the faithful from being terrified by their own small number.

Ellicott finds a second play on words at the opening of the next verse, since the term rendered sea coast may also mean an apportioned inheritance, so that the clause may read, it shall be for an inheritance to the remnant of the house of Judah. He calls the allusion to the captivity of Judah and its termination remarkable, and quotes the question who but the one in whose hand human wills are could then foresee that Judah would rebel like the ten tribes and be carried away, and yet return. On the visiting he notes that the verb is used for their relief and not their punishment, plain from the context though rare in itself; Wesley says the same.

Where the promise was made good is answered from the later history. Gill takes it of the return from Babylon, fulfilled in the times of the Maccabees when the rebuilt cities of Palestine fell into Jewish hands, and evident again in the times of the apostles, when Gaza and Ashdod were inhabited by Jews; he allows a further accomplishment in the latter day. Clarke agrees that the Maccabees finally accomplished what the prophets had predicted against that people, who lost their polity and were obliged at last to receive circumcision. Keil and Delitzsch marks where the threat turns from the Philistines in the west to the two nations that come next.
8:
Why these two are taken together is answered from their descent. Gill notes that both came from Lot and are mentioned together as being of the same cast and complexion; Henry adds that their countries joined and both adjoined Israel. Calvin presses the kinship harder: the connection ought to have turned them to mercy, yet they always infested the Jews with greater fury than others, and as it were with savage cruelty.

The charge itself is abusive speech. Ellicott defines the word as abusive speech, or offensive design expressed in words, and says the appeal of Balak to Balaam to come and curse this people at once suggests itself. Henry observes that the reproach ran both ways: while God's people kept close to their duty they were reproached for the singularities of their religion, and now that they had revolted they were reproached for that too, so that it has been their common lot in all ages to be reproached upon one account or another. Thus the old serpent spits his venom, he says, and pride is at the bottom of it. He draws the rule that if God hears the reproaches we are under, that is reason enough for us to be as a deaf man who hears not.

Calvin insists the words are God's and not the people's. Some take the sentence as spoken by the faithful, but the context requires it to be ascribed to God, who reminds them that he looked down from on high on the proud vauntings of Moab. The consolation was seasonable: the Jews saw these nations burning with fury when they had not been provoked, and making gain out of the calamities of a miserable people, and could only ask where God now was. On the injury itself Calvin says there is not so much bitterness in a hundred deaths as in one reproach, especially when the wicked triumph with the applauding consent of the whole world, for then all difference between good and evil is confounded. Gill says the Lord heard it and put it down in the book of his remembrance.

The oath that follows is weighed by two of them. Gill says the Lord swears by his own life, partly to show how grievously he resented the injuries done to his people and partly to make the fulfilment certain, his word and oath being immutable. Calvin observes that God undertakes their cause as though his anger were kindled; not that passions belong to him, but such a form of speaking expresses what the faithful could never otherwise conceive, his unspeakable love towards them. He also notes the two titles, the first exalting his power, the second his goodness, because he had adopted them as his own.

The sentence pronounced borrows the older ruin. Henry says they shall be as Sodom and Gomorrah, whose marks in the Dead Sea lay near their countries, not by fire from heaven but almost in the same manner; and that Israel should possess their lands, so that proud men, by the just judgment of God, fall under the mortification of being trampled on by those whom they once trampled on. Ellicott prefers an inheritance of nettles and finds the comparison the more apt because Lot, the ancestor of these nations, had lived in Sodom and narrowly escaped its destruction; he dates one devastation to Nebuchadnezzar, probably in revenge for the murder of Gedaliah, but holds the allusion here to be to some later and more permanent work, since the national existence of both had ceased long before the Christian era. Calvin limits the resemblance to the completeness of the overthrow rather than its manner, since their habitation was not to become a pool of water but a place where the bramble grows and salt may be dug; Clarke and Wesley say the land would lie uncultivated and fit only to dig salt out of.
10:
The reason given is pride. Gill remarks that it often goes before a fall and has ruined kingdoms as well as particular persons, and that it seems to have been the first sin of the apostate angels and of fallen man; Clarke refers back to the reproach already charged.

Whom the next words make afraid is disputed. Gill takes them of the Moabites and Ammonites, whose proud hearts the Lord would make tremble; but he reports the alternative of Kimchi, that it may be understood of the people of God, by whom the Lord is to be feared with a godly and filial fear, so that the clause would read that the Lord is to be feared by them, as the Targum inclines to take it. Calvin refuses the change. He grants that some render the word to be feared and take the next phrase as referring forward to the gods of the earth, a pronoun set before its noun, but calls this forced, since Moab and Ammon are evidently meant. He also declines to extend the verse to gospel times, the subject in hand being God's judgment.

The famishing of the gods is explained from the sacrifices themselves. Clarke says idolaters supposed their gods actually fed on the fumes rising from the burnt-offerings made to them, so the threat is of a worship entirely destroyed; Wesley puts it as the taking away of their sacrifices and drink-offerings. Ellicott gives the literal sense as to make lean. Calvin takes the verb metaphorically for consuming, and turns the figure round: there was a famine the idols had occasioned through the whole world, and God's own glory would exterminate whatever glory they had obtained. The point, he says, is that the wicked now disregard his power but shall find how terrible an avenger of his people he is.

Where the worship will be offered divides the last clause. Ellicott finds it difficult to accept the pregnant construction which would make it each one coming from his place to Jerusalem, as Keil and Delitzsch takes it, and concludes that this is one of the very few passages foretelling that the worship of Jehovah shall find centres outside the Holy Land, the usual prediction representing the converted nations as flowing to Jerusalem. Wesley says it shortly, not only at Jerusalem but everywhere. Calvin reads it as a promise of distance overcome, that however remote the countries, this would be no hindrance to God's name being celebrated there.

The turn to the Ethiopians is read as an argument from the far to the near. Gill narrows the name, taking it not of the Ethiopians in Africa beyond Egypt but of the inhabitants of Arabia Chusea, who lay near Moab and Ammon. Calvin makes the reasoning explicit: if God punished a nation so remote, how could Moab and Ammon escape, whose hatred was less excusable because they were related to the children of Abraham. Keil and Delitzsch reads the verse structurally, as naming two powerful nations to prove that the whole heathen world will succumb, and notes that for the south the prophet passes over Edom and Egypt.

The sword is identified and the history traced. Henry calls Nebuchadnezzar God's sword, the instrument by which these enemies were subdued, and recalls that the Ethiopians had once been a terror to Israel; Wesley and Clarke say as much of the Chaldeans. Ellicott thinks the pairing of Ethiopia with Assyria was suggested by an earlier prophecy, and traces what followed: Ethiopia suffering perhaps as an ally of Egypt after Carchemish, then reduced to vassalage by Cambyses, and under Xerxes obliged to furnish a contingent against the Greeks. Calvin notices that the prophet begins by summoning the Ethiopians in the second person and then continues in the third; some would emend the text, but he holds such changes to be common in this prophet.
13:
The turn northward is briefly explained. Gill says the hand is either the Lord's or Nebuchadnezzar's, his sword, who having subdued the nations to the south would lead his army north against Assyria; Wesley notes that it lay northward of Judea and due north from Babylon. Calvin gives the reason for going on: the Moabites and Ammonites were fans only, since they could not do much harm by their own strength, and it was they who stirred up the Assyrians and the remote nations, so that no enemy of the church would be left unpunished. He also observes that the person changes, God having spoken of his own sword in the verse before and the prophet speaking of him in the third person here, and reads the stretching out of the hand as saying that the Lord knows his own time and will put forth his power when needful.

What became of the city is told two ways. Calvin traces a decline rather than a single blow: Nineveh was the metropolis of the empire before the Assyrians were conquered by the Babylonians, and when Babylon recovered the sovereignty it had lost, Nineveh, though not demolished, lost its ruling power and gradually its name and wealth until it was a waste, the building of Ctesiphon proving its ruin. Clarke states the end result, that it was so completely destroyed that its situation is not now even known, the city of Mossoul being supposed to stand near where it once was.

Which creatures are named in the ruin is not settled. Clarke gives the two Hebrew words and reports that Newcome renders them the pelican and the porcupine. Ellicott prefers the pelican and the hedgehog, lodging on the pillar capitals as these lie strewn upon the ground; he renders the next clause as the voice of the bird singing in the windows, and quotes the remark that amid the muteness of the hedgehog and the loneliness of the solitary pelican, the spectator is startled by the glad strain of some song bird, unconscious that it sits in the windows of those at whose name the world grew pale. Calvin declines a laborious research into the kinds, since it is enough to know the prophet's design; Wesley keeps the bittern, as a bird that delights in desolate places.

Clarke has the windows demolished and wild fowl nesting in them, while the fine cedar ceilings are left open to the weather and crumble to dust; and he sets beside it a couplet from a Persian poet, that the spider holds the veil in the palace of Caesar and the owl stands sentinel in the watchtower of Afrasiab. Ellicott makes the same point in a line, that the desolation extends even to the cedar panelling of the roofless walls, laid open to wind and rain.

The flocks in the streets complete the reversal. Gill places them in streets where houses had stood and people had walked in great numbers, so that only shepherds' cottages and sheep feeding would be seen, as had been said already of the Philistine coast. Calvin makes the same contrast: while men were so many there was no place for flocks, least of all in the middle of a city so celebrated. He adds that beasts which shun the sight of men come forth when they find a country deserted, as after a slaughter in war, when a region is emptied of its inhabitants and the wolves and lions roam at full liberty; so wild beasts would come from remote places and find a home where Nineveh once stood. And he states why the picture was drawn for the Jews at all: that they might patiently bear their own miseries, understanding that God would become their defender, which he says is the only support that remains under very grievous evils, as Paul also reminds us.
15:
Whose voice closes the chapter is left open. Gill offers both, that these are the words of the prophet concluding his prophecy by a foresight of the ruin, or else the words of passengers, and what they would say when they saw the place lying in ruins. Wesley takes the first, and says the prophet triumphs over her.

What the city had been is described from its confidence. Gill calls it once exceeding populous, its inhabitants full of mirth and gaiety, abounding with wealth and indulging themselves in all carnal delights, and, being well fortified, careless and unconcerned, imagining their city impregnable. Clarke says the same shortly, that mirth, jocularity and pleasure reigned there without interruption; and on the closing gesture he notes that the passer-by will point her out as a mark and monument of divine displeasure.

Ellicott traces the language rather than the history. He holds that the earlier part of the verse is doubtless based on the words of Isaiah to one given to pleasures, who dwells carelessly and says in her heart that she is, and none else beside her; and that the remainder recalls the closing words of two other prophecies against great cities.

Calvin reads the whole verse as anticipation. It seems to him added lest the magnificent splendour of Nineveh should frighten the Jews, as though the city were exempt from all danger; and his answer is that the very greatness on which Nineveh prided itself would be the cause of its ruin, since it would cast itself down by its own pride. He puts it in a figure: as a wall, when it swells, will not long stand, so men, when they inwardly swell and vent their own boastings, burst, and though no one pushes them down they fall of themselves. He observes that Isaiah reprobates the pride of Babylon in nearly the same words, and that what was said there of Babylon is justly transferred here to Nineveh.

Why the picture was set before the Jews at all he then explains. We are seized with wonder, he says, when anything grand and splendid presents itself to us; so the prophet exhibits Nineveh already in its state of ruin, lest the power of that city should dazzle their eyes. Behold, he has him say, you see this city full of exultation resting as in a state of safety, conscious of no fear, regarding itself exempt from the common lot of men as though it were built in the clouds; but let not a frail and evanescent splendour terrify you, for God will in his own time reduce it to nothing.

The boast itself Calvin takes as the stated cause of the fall. By saying that she is, and there is none beside her, the prophet means that Nineveh was so blinded by its splendour that it defied every change of fortune. Had Babylon spoken so it would have been no wonder, he remarks, for Babylon had taken the sovereignty from Nineveh; but the same pride infatuates peoples as well as kings, since each thinks himself great alone and looks on others as though they were placed beneath his feet. In few words, then, the cause of the ruin is given: the city thought its condition on the earth fixed and perpetual. Calvin makes the example a common one, that God cannot endure the presumption of men who, inflated by their own greatness, do not think themselves to be men nor humble themselves suitably, but forget themselves as though they could rise above the heavens; and he closes by saying that if we desire to be protected by God's hand we should bear in mind what our condition is, and daily, yea hourly, prepare ourselves for a change.
